parts:
Yes. I’d separate these two issues, because the medication list actually becomes much clearer once we distinguish “old symptomatic self-treatment” from “new plan from the allergist.”

1. Did she mean all steroids?

I would NOT interpret “after stopping dexamethasone” as automatically meaning “stop every steroid in every form.”

The strongest clue is the prescription itself: the doctor prescribed Ryaltris, which contains mometasone — an intranasal corticosteroid — together with olopatadine. citeturn739254view3 So unless she explicitly said otherwise, it would be strange to read her instruction as “also stop the nasal steroid I’ve just prescribed.”

There is one important exception: Pulmicort.

Pulmicort is an inhaled corticosteroid, and inhaled corticosteroid treatment can make asthma harder to confirm objectively; FeNO in particular is steroid-responsive. GINA explicitly prefers asthma testing before starting ICS when possible. citeturn780148search0turn780148search8

So my interpretation would be:

- Dexamethasone: definitely stop according to her plan.
- Ryaltris: probably continue exactly as prescribed; it already contains nasal mometasone.
- Pulmicort: this is the one I would clarify before FeNO, because intermittent use could influence the result.
- Skin steroid creams, if she uses any: irrelevant to ALEX/FeNO in the ordinary sense; they mainly become relevant if skin testing is being done on treated skin.
- ALEX3 is a blood specific-IgE test, so this is not analogous to skin-prick testing where antihistamines suppress the skin response. ALEX itself measures serum total/specific IgE. citeturn671295search6

I would send/call the clinic with just one very concrete question:

“Перед FeNO Лада іноді користувалась Пульмікортом. Його теж потрібно не використовувати перед тестом? А Ріалтріс продовжувати за призначеною схемою?”

That removes the ambiguity without turning it into a pharmacology debate.

And importantly: if she actually needs Pulmicort/Berodual because breathing becomes significantly worse, I would not withhold needed respiratory treatment merely to get a prettier FeNO result. GINA makes the same general point: diagnostic purity comes second when treatment is clinically necessary. citeturn780148search8


2. How I would merge the medication lists

I would NOT simply append the new drugs to everything she was already taking. There are several obvious overlaps.

Here is how I would understand it:

| Before the allergist | New plan | What I’d do |
|---|---|---|
| Dexamethasone | Rupafin (rupatadine) | **Dexamethasone is being stopped; Rupafin is the new systemic antihistamine strategy** |
| Cetrin or L-Cet | Rupafin | **Probably replaced by Rupafin**, not added on top |
| Suprastin at night | Rupafin | **Probably replaced by Rupafin**, unless doctor explicitly said to continue |
| Glenspray Active | Ryaltris | **Replace with Ryaltris**, not use both |
| Tizin at night | Ryaltris | I would **not automatically continue Tizin** unless doctor told her to |
| Pulmicort + Berodual occasionally | No equivalent respiratory drug prescribed | **Needs clarification**, especially before FeNO / if wheezing recurs |
| — | Opatanol eye drops | Add according to prescription |
| — | EpiPen 0.3 mg | Add as emergency medication; carry it |
| Contraceptive | — | Continue as before unless another doctor says otherwise |
| Omega-3 | — | Same |

The nasal-spray substitution is particularly clear pharmacologically. **Glenspray Active already contains mometasone + azelastine**, while **Ryaltris contains mometasone + olopatadine**. Using both would duplicate the nasal corticosteroid and broadly duplicate the antihistamine component. citeturn150920search1turn739254view3

Similarly, Rupafin, Cetrin/L-Cet and Suprastin are all systemic antihistamine approaches. Given what you were explicitly told — Rupafin was prescribed to manage symptoms while getting her off dexamethasone — I would treat Rupafin as the current oral antihistamine regimen rather than casually stacking the old tablets on top.

So, unless the doctor told you something different, I’d rewrite Lada’s “current medication” list now as:

- Rupafin 10 mg — according to the prescribed 30 → 20 → 10 mg/day schedule.
- Ryaltris nasal spray — according to the prescribed schedule.
- Opatanol eye drops — according to the prescription.
- EpiPen 0.3 mg — emergency use.
- Contraceptive — unchanged.
- Omega-3 — unchanged.
- Pulmicort + Berodual — **status unclear; ask specifically whether/how she should use them before the respiratory work-up.**

And I’d move Dexamethasone, Cetrin/L-Cet, Suprastin, Glenspray Active and Tizin into a little mental bucket called “previous treatment,” rather than continuing them by default.

The one thing I would verify with the allergist is **Pulmicort/Berodual**. Everything else looks much more like a replacement regimen than an additive one.

parts:
Tizin, Glenspray, Suprastin, Pulmicort + Berodual 
Okay that's my mistake. I should have clarified this in the list above. Lada says that basically all this medication is essential for her because she feels bad without it, especially the first one. Also she just tried this nasal spray that the doctor prescribed and she is saying that its effect is worse than the effect of Tizin
Also she is saying that she is taking Tizin 3+ 2x into each nostril, Glenspray 2x day, Pulmicort + Berodual each other day or less when cant get asleep after many hours

My question here is that she does need to control her symptoms, and she has this quite substantial list of self-prescribed medication. The doctor suggested a substitution but we're not sure if the substitution will work, to what extent it is expected to work, and whether the medication the doctor prescribed would not work as well as the one she was taking.

What to do with this list? We should obviously eliminate the list of self-prescribed medication. What part could be preserved in case symptoms are really bad?

thoughts.content: I’m comparing the prescribed sprays with Tizin: if Tizin contains xylometazoline or oxymetazoline, frequent use and worsening congestion without it can indicate rebound congestion. I’d verify the active ingredient and advise prompt clinician review rather than increasing doses.

thoughts.content: I’d avoid keeping overlapping sprays or adding Suprastin independently. Ryaltris may need regular use, while Tizin can cause rebound congestion if overused. Preserve only the prescribed plan, confirm Tizin’s ingredient, and contact the prescriber urgently about the severe dependence on it.

parts:
Yes. This changes the picture quite a bit.

I would not “delete” the old list. I’d split it into two concepts:

Current treatment = what the allergist has now prescribed.
Previous/self-directed treatment = important history, especially because it tells the doctor how severe the symptoms actually are.

The second list matters because needing Tizin constantly and Pulmicort/Berodual every few nights is clinically meaningful.

The key issue: Tizin

Before making a definite call, check the bottle and tell me its active ingredient. If it is Tizin Xylo / xylometazoline, then what you describe is a red flag.

If by “3+ 2x into each nostril” you mean roughly 2 sprays per nostril 3+ times per day, and this has been going on for more than several days, that is far beyond how topical xylometazoline is normally intended to be used. Prolonged use can itself produce rebound nasal congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa), where the nose becomes extremely blocked when the drug wears off. The UK medicines regulator specifically warns about this with xylometazoline/oxymetazoline. citeturn566787search2

That could explain the apparent paradox:

“I absolutely need Tizin because without it I can’t breathe.”

Part of that may be her original allergic rhinitis, but part may now be congestion produced by repeated decongestant use itself.

And this also explains why one dose of Ryaltris feels “worse.” Tizin rapidly constricts blood vessels and physically opens the nose. Ryaltris is olopatadine + mometasone; it treats the allergic process rather than giving the same immediate vasoconstrictor sensation. citeturn566787search1

So I would not conclude after one use that Ryaltris has failed.

What I would do with each old drug

- Tizin: do not treat it as the fallback medication indefinitely. First check the exact formulation. If it is xylometazoline/another topical decongestant and she has been using it this heavily, I would contact the allergist and specifically ask for a plan to get her off it. I would not invent an abrupt-stop versus taper schedule ourselves.
- Glenspray Active: I would not use it together with Ryaltris unless the doctor explicitly says so. Glenspray Active contains mometasone + azelastine; Ryaltris contains mometasone + olopatadine, so there is substantial duplication. citeturn390241search10turn566787search1
- Suprastin: I would not preserve it routinely on top of Rupafin. Rupafin is now the planned oral antihistamine. And for a severe reaction, Suprastin is not the rescue medication — epinephrine is.
- Pulmicort + Berodual: this is the one I would NOT simply throw away from the story. Using nebulized respiratory medication roughly every other night because she cannot sleep from breathing symptoms is important evidence that her lower-airway symptoms need a proper plan. GINA recommends that people with asthma have a defined reliever strategy rather than repeatedly improvising treatment when symptoms become bad. citeturn566787search3turn390241search24
- Dexamethasone: follow the allergist’s plan to stop it rather than preserving it as an emergency fallback.

So the “active medication” list would now be Rupafin, Ryaltris, Opatanol, EpiPen, plus her unrelated regular medicines.

But I would add one separate sentence to her history:

“До консультації самостійно використовувала Тизин часто (уточнити дозу/тривалість), Гленспрей Актив 2 рази на день, Супрастин на ніч та Пульмікорт + Беродуал приблизно через день або рідше через нічні проблеми з диханням.”

That is much more useful medically than pretending those drugs vanished after today's appointment.

What I would clarify with the doctor now

There are really only two unresolved medication questions, and I think they're worth contacting the clinic about rather than waiting a month:

1. “She has actually been using Tizin very frequently and feels unable to breathe normally without it. What is the intended transition from Tizin to Ryaltris — should it be stopped immediately or reduced somehow?”

2. “She has been using Pulmicort + Berodual approximately every other night when breathing prevents her from sleeping. Until the FeNO/asthma work-up, what should she use when those symptoms occur?”

Those are not nitpicky questions. They are information the doctor apparently did not have when she wrote today's plan.

And I would particularly avoid solving #2 ourselves. Pulmicort and Berodual are doing very different things, and “a nebulizer combination whenever I eventually can't sleep” is not a good substitute for an actual asthma/bronchospasm action plan. Her frequency of respiratory symptoms makes that worth clarifying promptly. citeturn566787search3

One more important thing: if her nighttime breathing ever resembles her anaphylactic episodes — throat/tongue swelling, hoarse voice, rapidly worsening breathing, generalized itching/hives, dizziness, etc. — that is a different pathway: follow the new EpiPen/emergency plan rather than trying Pulmicort/Berodual and waiting.

If you send me a photo/name of the exact Tizin bottle and roughly how long she has been using it at that frequency, I can be much more specific about that part.

parts:
Yes. Given that it is Tizin Xylo (xylometazoline), she uses it heavily, and she has already had trouble stopping it before, I would treat this as very likely rebound congestion/rhinitis medicamentosa on top of her underlying allergy. With prolonged use, the spray itself can make the nose increasingly blocked when it wears off, which creates exactly the “I cannot function without it” cycle. citeturn612675view0

### What I would do now

I would not try to preserve the old regimen. I’d make the allergist’s treatment the base:

- Rupatadine — exactly as prescribed.
- Ryaltris — exactly as prescribed and consistently, not judged by one or two doses.
- Opatanol — as prescribed.
- EpiPen — emergency medication.
- Stop dexamethasone as the allergist instructed.

Ryaltris contains olopatadine + mometasone and treats the allergic inflammation; it is not pharmacologically equivalent to the almost immediate vasoconstriction from Tizin. So it can feel much less dramatic even when it is doing the more appropriate long-term job. citeturn612675view1

### The exception: Tizin

Because her use is already very heavy, **I would not simply say “throw it away tonight and suffer.”** The MHRA specifically advises gradual withdrawal in people who have become reliant on xylometazoline, because abrupt stopping can temporarily make the congestion much worse. citeturn612675view0

A reasonable temporary strategy, if you cannot reach a doctor, is the **one-nostril method**:

1. Continue Ryaltris in both nostrils exactly as prescribed.
2. Pick one nostril and **stop Tizin completely on that side**.
3. If she genuinely cannot cope without Tizin initially, use it only in the other nostril, trying not to increase the amount or frequency.
4. Once the untreated side becomes tolerable, discontinue Tizin from the remaining side too.

Using one nostril at a time is an established clinical weaning approach for rebound congestion, although there isn't one universally proven taper schedule. citeturn896670search0

So I would think of Tizin as a **short bridge out of Tizin**, not as the fallback treatment whenever Ryaltris feels weaker.

Saline nasal spray or rinsing can also help during the transition and does not cause rebound congestion. citeturn612675view4

### What to expect

The first few days may be unpleasant. With withdrawal plus an intranasal corticosteroid, subjective rebound symptoms can improve within a few days, while the nasal tissue itself may take longer to settle; chronic cases can take considerably longer. citeturn612675view2

So this is important:

**“Ryaltris doesn't open my nose as powerfully as Tizin” ≠ “Ryaltris isn't working.”**

Tizin has trained the comparison against an extremely fast decongestant effect.

### What I would NOT preserve from the old list

- **Glenspray Active:** don't combine routinely with Ryaltris. They substantially overlap therapeutically, including a nasal corticosteroid.
- **Suprastin:** I wouldn't routinely stack it onto the prescribed rupatadine unless a clinician specifically tells her to.
- **Dexamethasone:** don't keep it as an emergency allergy medication; follow the allergist's plan to stop it.

### Pulmicort + Berodual is different

This one shouldn't be folded into the Tizin problem.

If she needs Pulmicort + Berodual roughly every other night because **wheezing/chest tightness/shortness of breath keeps her from sleeping**, that's a lower-airway problem and needs its own plan. Ryaltris and Tizin treat the nose; they don't solve asthma/bronchospasm.

Since you can't reach this allergist easily, I would try to clarify that part with **another clinician or pharmacist/primary-care doctor soon**, rather than inventing a long-term Pulmicort/Berodual schedule yourselves.

And if what she calls “can't breathe” means significant wheezing, chest tightness, difficulty speaking, worsening shortness of breath, or throat/tongue swelling, **don't treat that by taking more Tizin and waiting**. With her history, respiratory symptoms need to be distinguished from simple nasal obstruction.

So my practical medication picture right now would be:

**New regimen = base treatment.  
Tizin = temporary structured withdrawal only.  
Glenspray/Suprastin = don't routinely add back.  
Pulmicort + Berodual = unresolved separate respiratory issue that deserves clarification.**

Given how heavily she uses Tizin, I also think an ENT visit would be quite reasonable if withdrawal is very difficult or the nose remains severely obstructed despite the new treatment. Long-standing decongestant overuse can coexist with other causes of obstruction that are worth actually looking for. citeturn612675view0

parts:
Yes — given the timing and severity, I would change course rather than blindly follow the 30 mg schedule.

### ⚠️ First: make sure this isn't another allergic reaction

Light-headedness and nausea can be medication side effects, but with Lada's history they can also occur during a serious allergic reaction.

If she has any of these now — worsening breathing/wheezing, throat or tongue swelling, hoarse voice, widespread hives/itching, repeated vomiting, fainting/near-fainting, or rapidly worsening weakness — **use the emergency plan the allergist gave her and seek emergency help.** Antihistamines or dexamethasone are not substitutes for epinephrine in anaphylaxis. citeturn439090search25turn439090search6

### If it is mainly dizziness + nausea + sleepiness

Those are all recognized adverse effects of rupatadine: sleepiness and dizziness are common, and nausea is reported as well. citeturn439090search28turn158674search17

And she took **30 mg**, while the licensed adult dose is 10 mg once daily. Her allergist deliberately prescribed a higher short-term dose, but that makes a significant side effect more plausible. citeturn158674search1

Given that she describes the symptoms as pretty bad, **I would not give her another 30 mg dose until you have spoken to a clinician or pharmacist.** That is different from saying the allergist's prescription was wrong; it means she appears not to be tolerating the prescribed high dose.

I would try, today, in this order:

1. allergist/clinic;
2. pharmacist who can see the actual prescription;
3. another doctor/urgent-care service if you can't reach either.

Tell them very specifically: **“She took rupatadine 30 mg as prescribed and developed substantial dizziness/light-headedness, nausea and prolonged sleepiness. Should we reduce to 20/10 mg or change antihistamine?”**

That is the actual decision you need them to make.

### I would NOT use dexamethasone to compensate

I wouldn't do:

“Rupatadine makes her feel bad → skip it → take dexamethasone instead.”

The allergist was specifically trying to move her away from systemic dexamethasone, and corticosteroids aren't appropriate rescue treatment for anaphylaxis. citeturn439090search30

From what you've told me, she had been taking dexamethasone for only around **four days**. For systemic glucocorticoid courses shorter than 3–4 weeks, Endocrine Society guidance generally says tapering isn't necessary because clinically important adrenal suppression is unlikely. citeturn158674search0

So **I would follow the plan to stop dexamethasone rather than keep taking intermittent doses**, assuming four days really is her total recent course. If she had actually been taking it repeatedly for weeks before that, tell me — that changes the answer.

### For today

Until the dizziness resolves:

- no driving;
- avoid alcohol;
- I would **not add Suprastin or another sedating antihistamine on top of the rupatadine** without advice;
- drink normally and eat something if she can;
- if you have a blood-pressure cuff, checking BP and pulse is useful information to give the clinician, but a normal reading doesn't prove everything is fine.

One extra thing worth checking: **no grapefruit/grapefruit juice** around the rupatadine — it can substantially increase rupatadine exposure. citeturn158674search1

So my practical answer is: **don't force the next 30 mg dose through significant adverse effects, don't substitute dexamethasone on your own, and get same-day medication advice about lowering/changing the rupatadine regimen.**

If you tell me exactly **when she took the three tablets, when the dizziness began, and her dexamethasone dose**, I can help judge how well the timing fits a rupatadine adverse effect.

parts: Okay we scheduled a consultation with the same doctor, but only for tomorrow evening. We need to decide what to do today so I asked her to give me an update on her symptoms in the order that would reflect the most significant ones, and she said she she doesn't feel like it's another severe allergy episode for sure so her most significant complaint pain in her lungs. She's describing it as her usual symptoms during seasonal allergy but now it's pretty pronounced. Then fatigue and she says that this one, especially that pronounced one, isn't usual for her so she says that it's something new and probably related to the new drug. Headache and again it's something new. And a little bit of nausea and again she says it's something And a little bit of lightheadead.  bottom line, yesterday lightheadedness and nausea were pretty severe but now they're sort of better. They're still present. Overall she feels shitty and we need something like a plan for the next 24 hours in terms of medication.

thoughts.content: I’m treating chest or “lung” pain with breathing symptoms as potentially urgent, not merely an antihistamine side effect. I’d advise same-day medical assessment and avoiding additional antihistamine doses until a clinician or pharmacist reviews the reaction.

parts:
Given the update, I would make the next 24 hours intentionally boring: avoid adding more drugs, avoid another high-dose rupatadine exposure, and make sure the chest/lung symptom is not being underestimated.

What worries me most today

The fatigue, headache, dizziness and nausea fit known rupatadine adverse effects quite well; somnolence, headache, fatigue and dizziness are among its recognized adverse effects, and nausea is also reported. citeturn643788search0turn643788search20

But **“pain in the lungs” is the part I would not attribute to rupatadine.** If by that she means pronounced chest pain, worsening chest tightness, or painful breathing — particularly together with wheezing or shortness of breath — I would get her assessed today rather than waiting until tomorrow evening. GINA advises early urgent assessment when respiratory symptoms are worsening. citeturn643788search2

⚠️ And if throat/tongue swelling, increasing hoarseness, rapidly worsening breathing, widespread hives/itching, fainting or another clear anaphylactic pattern appears, follow the EpiPen/emergency plan from yesterday rather than this medication plan.

For the next 24 hours

Assuming her breathing is stable and the chest sensation is her familiar seasonal symptom rather than significant/new chest pain:

1. **I would hold the next rupatadine dose today.**

I would particularly not repeat **30 mg** while she still has substantial new fatigue/headache plus residual dizziness and nausea from the previous dose.

That doesn't mean rupatadine has to be abandoned permanently. Tomorrow the allergist can decide whether to restart at 10 mg, 20 mg, switch antihistamines, or do something else.

Importantly, skipping an antihistamine dose does not remove some protective shield against anaphylaxis — antihistamines are symptom-control drugs, not substitutes for epinephrine in preventing/treating a severe reaction.

2. **I would not take more dexamethasone to replace it.**

The whole reason the allergist introduced the new regimen was to get her away from repeated systemic dexamethasone.

Based on what you've told me — roughly four days of dexamethasone use — endocrine guidelines generally do not require tapering for courses shorter than 3–4 weeks. citeturn643788search3

So unless there is some longer steroid use we haven't accounted for, I would **not take another dexamethasone dose today merely because rupatadine is being held**.

3. **Continue Ryaltris as prescribed if she is tolerating it.**

I wouldn't bring Glenspray back on top of it.

One thing worth knowing for tomorrow: Ryaltris itself contains the antihistamine olopatadine as well as mometasone, and it can occasionally cause sleepiness. Its prescribing information also warns that combining it with other antihistamines can increase antihistamine adverse effects. citeturn936333view0turn936333view2

That doesn't mean the doctor made a mistake prescribing Ryaltris + rupatadine. But it gives you another useful question tomorrow: whether the **combined antihistamine load** may have contributed to how awful she felt.

I would therefore definitely **not add Suprastin, Cetrin or L-Cet today** on top of the residual rupatadine/Ryaltris.

4. **Tizin Xylo: don't escalate it today.**

Given her dependence/rebound-congestion situation, I also wouldn't choose today — while she already feels terrible — for a heroic abrupt withdrawal.

Use the smallest amount she can manage with, don't increase beyond her existing use, keep using Ryaltris, and discuss an actual Tizin exit strategy tomorrow.

And Tizin should only be thought of as a nasal decongestant here — **not treatment for the chest/lung symptoms.**

5. **Pulmicort + Berodual is where I wouldn't improvise.**

Because she is now reporting pronounced chest/lung symptoms, I don't want to tell you over chat to take or withhold a nebulized respiratory combination that she has been self-directing.

If the chest tightness/wheezing becomes bad enough tonight that she feels she needs Pulmicort + Berodual just to breathe or sleep, **I'd treat that as a reason for same-day medical assessment rather than wait until tomorrow's allergist appointment.**

What I would monitor today

If you have the equipment, record temperature, pulse, blood pressure and oxygen saturation, plus roughly when each symptom improves/worsens. Don't obsess over the numbers; they're mainly useful context for tomorrow.

She should also avoid driving and alcohol while she is dizzy/sleepy. Rupatadine can impair alertness in some people, and Ryaltris can occasionally add somnolence. citeturn643788search0turn936333view2

So my practical medication sheet for tonight would be:

- **Rupatadine: HOLD today pending tomorrow's review**
- **Dexamethasone: don't take another dose as a substitute**
- Ryaltris: continue prescribed dose if tolerated
- Opatanol: continue as prescribed if needed
- Suprastin / Cetrin / L-Cet / Glenspray: don't add back
- Tizin Xylo: minimum necessary, don't escalate; deal with withdrawal separately
- Pulmicort + Berodual: don't invent a new dosing plan; substantial respiratory symptoms → assessment today
- EpiPen: available for the emergency symptoms the allergist discussed

The fact that yesterday's severe dizziness/nausea are **improving today** is somewhat reassuring and makes a medication adverse effect more plausible, but the pronounced chest/lung complaint is the part I would use to decide whether she can reasonably wait for tomorrow.

If you can describe what she means by **“pain in her lungs”** — pain versus pressure/tightness, whether breathing deeply makes it hurt, and whether she currently has wheezing or breathlessness — I can help you make that particular wait-versus-go-today decision more sensibly.

parts:
I would not use “half a dexamethasone dose” as the compromise here.

Why

She has taken about 0.5 mg twice daily for ~5 days, so roughly 1 mg/day. For a glucocorticoid course this short, current Endocrine Society guidance says a taper is generally not needed; courses under 3–4 weeks can usually be stopped without tapering because clinically important adrenal suppression is unlikely. citeturn552816search0turn552816search7

So taking 0.5 mg today and again tomorrow would not be serving an endocrine “taper” purpose. It would mainly be continuing systemic steroid treatment for symptom relief.

And systemic corticosteroids are not normally a good maintenance/rescue strategy for allergic rhinitis; guidelines favor intranasal corticosteroid-based treatment and reserve systemic steroids for exceptional situations because the risk/benefit is worse. citeturn552816search2turn552816search3

What I would do today

Assuming she is stable, this does not feel like another anaphylactic episode, and the chest discomfort really is her familiar seasonal symptom:

- Hold the rupatadine today because the new fatigue, headache, dizziness and nausea appeared after the high dose and are recognized rupatadine adverse effects. citeturn552816search40turn552816search24
- Do not take dexamethasone merely to “replace” the rupatadine or create a taper.
- Continue Ryaltris and Opatanol according to the allergist’s prescription if she tolerates them.
- Don’t add Suprastin/Cetrin/L-Cet on top today.
- Keep Tizin to the minimum she can tolerate while you deal with that dependence separately.
- Tomorrow, give the allergist the exact story: 30 mg rupatadine → marked dizziness/nausea yesterday → persistent fatigue/headache/light-headedness today, and ask what lower dose or alternative they want.

One reason I’m especially not enthusiastic about another dexamethasone dose is that dexamethasone is long-acting. A single dose can exert glucocorticoid effects for well beyond the few hours in which she wants symptom relief. citeturn544404search6turn544404search14

The important distinction

If she is thinking:

“I need something because my nose/seasonal allergy is miserable”

then Ryaltris/Tizin-transition is the relevant problem.

If she is thinking:

“My lungs/chest are painful, tight, wheezy, and it’s hard to breathe”

then dexamethasone is not a good improvised rescue plan. That is the unresolved possible-asthma/bronchospasm issue, and if it becomes meaningfully worse tonight I would have her assessed rather than trying to bridge to tomorrow with steroid tablets.

So between your two options, my preference is:

**Skip both the 30 mg rupatadine and the dexamethasone today, continue the prescribed local allergy treatment, and reassess with the allergist tomorrow.**

The fact that yesterday’s severe nausea/light-headedness are already improving supports waiting out the suspected drug side effect rather than adding another systemic drug to the picture.

parts:
Yes — that’s a very plausible interpretation.

If she has now gone ~24 hours without Tizin despite previously feeling dependent on it, that strongly suggests the new regimen is doing something meaningful for the nasal allergy/congestion. Ryaltris itself can start helping nasal symptoms fairly quickly, and rupatadine also suppresses histamine-driven symptoms, so it may be the combination rather than rupatadine alone. citeturn717968search9turn717968search18

At the same time, the side-effect pattern you described fits rupatadine quite well: sleepiness, headache, fatigue and dizziness are recognized common adverse effects, and nausea is also reported. citeturn717968search1turn717968search25

So I’d summarize the situation for tomorrow’s doctor like this:

- **The new treatment seems effective for her nasal symptoms**: no Tizin for ~24 hours, which is a major change for her.
- **But 30 mg rupatadine seems poorly tolerated**: marked dizziness/nausea after the dose, followed by fatigue, headache and residual light-headedness the next day.
- The useful question is therefore probably not “does rupatadine work?” but **“can we keep the benefit at a lower dose or with a different antihistamine?”**

That distinction matters, because the doctor might reasonably decide to reduce the rupatadine dose rather than abandon the whole new treatment plan.

And I’d be careful not to credit all of the improvement to rupatadine: Ryaltris contains both olopatadine and mometasone and is specifically designed to control allergic rhinitis, so it may be doing a substantial part of the work too. citeturn717968search18turn717968search23

For today, the fact that she is tolerating being off Tizin is actually encouraging. I would avoid “testing” that by restarting it just because it used to be essential. If she can stay comfortable without it, that is exactly the direction you want.

Yes — if she reliably drops to 3–4 hours of sleep during these episodes, I’d bring this up explicitly tomorrow. That is enough insomnia to justify a short-term plan, especially because poor sleep can amplify stress and make every physical symptom harder to tolerate.

One important possibility is that the recent dexamethasone contributed. Insomnia and psychological activation are well-recognized systemic steroid effects, often appearing within days of starting treatment; taking dexamethasone later in the day makes sleep disruption more likely. citeturn321493search3turn550246search0

### What I’d ask the doctor about

For her situation, I’d think in this order:

- **First choice to discuss: melatonin.** It is relatively gentle, does not suppress breathing the way stronger sedatives can, and is used for short-term insomnia, although effectiveness varies and prescribing conventions depend on age/country. Typical medical regimens use it shortly before bedtime rather than as an “as needed in the middle of the night” drug. citeturn550246search3turn550246search9
- If she genuinely has **severe short-term insomnia despite that**, doctors sometimes prescribe a very short course of a hypnotic such as **zopiclone or zolpidem**. NICE specifically reserves these kinds of drugs for severe insomnia and short courses because of tolerance/dependence and next-day impairment. citeturn321493search1turn321493search7
- Benzodiazepines can also sedate, but I would consider them a less attractive solution for recurring seasonal insomnia because of dependence/tolerance risks. NICE similarly restricts their use to severe, disabling insomnia. citeturn321493search7

### What I would avoid improvising

I would **not turn Suprastin into her sleeping pill** just because it is sedating.

Likewise, hydroxyzine is sometimes used for anxiety/sedation, but in her specific situation I don't love the idea of solving insomnia by stacking another sedating antihistamine onto a treatment plan that already involves rupatadine/Ryaltris and where she recently had pronounced medication-related sleepiness/dizziness. Rupatadine's product information warns that interactions with CNS depressants cannot be excluded. citeturn321493search11 Hydroxyzine also has a recognized QT-prolongation risk, so it's not as innocuous as “an antihistamine that makes you sleepy.” citeturn806607search0

I also wouldn't use dexamethasone to get through these periods — ironically, **it may be contributing to the insomnia rather than helping it**. citeturn321493search10

### The question I'd ask tomorrow

Something as simple as:

> “During bad allergy periods I often sleep only 3–4 hours a night for several days. What can I safely use short-term for sleep with this allergy treatment — would melatonin be enough, or do I need a short-course sleeping medication?”

And tell the doctor that this predates the new rupatadine, but that she's just had several days of dexamethasone. That distinction is useful.

One thing I'd watch for tonight/tomorrow: if “insomnia” is accompanied by **unusually elevated mood, feeling extremely wired despite almost no sleep, racing thoughts, marked agitation, impulsive/uncharacteristic behaviour, confusion, or hallucinations**, don't treat that as ordinary stress insomnia. Systemic steroids can occasionally cause substantial psychiatric activation, and that deserves prompt medical advice. citeturn550246search0turn550246search1

For ordinary “I am exhausted and anxious but can't fall asleep” insomnia, though, **melatonin versus a very short prescribed hypnotic course** is the discussion I would have with the allergist tomorrow, rather than adding another antihistamine.

parts:
Yes — I think “wait and see” is reasonable here, and I would not add an insomnia medication while she is already noticeably sleepy.

The new antihistamine could absolutely be contributing. Rupatadine commonly causes sleepiness; fatigue, headache and dizziness are also recognized side effects, and nausea can occur too. citeturn500532search0turn500532search1

At the same time, exhaustion is also plausible. She has had several days of poor sleep, a recent severe allergic episode, ongoing seasonal symptoms, and dexamethasone itself can cause insomnia. Once the steroid is stopped and the allergy symptoms come under better control, some “catch-up sleep” would not be surprising. citeturn500532search31

What I’d do now

- **Don’t add a sleeping pill just because insomnia was a problem a few days ago.**
- Let her sleep normally for a couple of nights and see where things settle.
- Tell the doctor that rupatadine appears to be helping the allergy symptoms but is also producing significant daytime sleepiness.
- Avoid driving, alcohol, Suprastin, sedatives or other things that could compound the drowsiness while she feels like this. Rupatadine’s product information specifically lists somnolence as its most common adverse effect. citeturn500532search0

I would also separate two goals:

**Good:** she can now sleep 7–9 hours at night instead of 3–4.

**Potential problem:** she is sleeping 7–9 hours and still feels heavily sedated, needs long daytime naps, has difficulty concentrating, or feels drugged.

If the second pattern persists as the rupatadine dose comes down, that is a reason to revisit the dose or antihistamine choice rather than adding another drug to manipulate sleep.

And I’d definitely mention to the doctor that the medication seems to have achieved two useful things at once: **her allergy symptoms are controlled enough that she stopped Tizin, and her severe insomnia has disappeared — but perhaps at the cost of too much sedation.** That gives them a much better basis for deciding whether a lower maintenance dose might preserve the benefit without making her sleepy all day.

parts:
Pregabalin can be a reasonable anti-anxiety drug in the right context, but I would push back on the idea that it is simply “a safer benzodiazepine.”

For generalized anxiety disorder, pregabalin has real evidence of efficacy and is used clinically; NICE, for example, suggests considering it when SSRIs/SNRIs are not tolerated. Benzodiazepines are generally reserved for short-term crises rather than routine GAD treatment. citeturn740019search0turn740019search16

But pregabalin is not dependence-free. UK regulators strengthened warnings in 2026 because pregabalin, benzodiazepines and Z-drugs all carry risks of dependence, withdrawal, tolerance and addiction. citeturn740019search1

In Lada’s current situation, I actually would not be very enthusiastic about adding it right now.

Why:

- she is already getting significant sleepiness/dizziness from the current antihistamine regimen;
- pregabalin itself very commonly causes dizziness and somnolence; citeturn550204search0turn550204search1
- it can also cause edema and weight gain, which is a particularly awkward match given that she already reported substantial swelling and ~3 kg weight gain after the recent episode. citeturn550204search3turn550204search7
- she has an unresolved respiratory issue/possible asthma, so I’d rather not casually add another CNS-depressing medication while the doctors are still sorting out why she sometimes has breathing trouble. Pregabalin has a recognized respiratory-depression warning, particularly in higher-risk situations or with other CNS depressants. citeturn740019search5

For insomnia specifically, I wouldn’t choose pregabalin just because it makes people sleepy. There is evidence that it can improve sleep in people with generalized anxiety disorder, but that is different from using it as a straightforward sleeping pill. citeturn543950search10

So I’d frame it like this:

**If she has a real recurring anxiety disorder that also drives insomnia**, pregabalin is a perfectly legitimate medication to discuss with a psychiatrist/doctor, especially if SSRIs/SNRIs are unsuitable.

**If the problem is simply several nights of insomnia during severe allergy periods**, I wouldn’t reach for pregabalin as the first solution. It is a relatively substantial long-term CNS medication for a potentially short-lived problem.

And right now, since rupatadine seems to have flipped her from 3–4 hours of sleep to daytime sleepiness, I’d be especially reluctant to add anything sedating. I’d first see where she lands after the antihistamine dose is stabilized.

So compared with benzodiazepines: **yes, pregabalin can be preferable for ongoing generalized anxiety in some patients; no, I would not consider it a generally safer or lower-risk substitute for occasional insomnia.** In Lada’s particular situation, the dizziness/somnolence + previous edema make me lean away from it unless there is a separate strong anxiety indication.

parts:
Okay it's been a couple of weeks and there is good news and bad news. Good news is that she switched completely to new medication and it does seem to work for her in terms of controlling her seasonal allergy symptoms. It probably works better than her previous combination of medication so she could sleep horizontally. Overall she seems to have fewer symptoms 

Bad news is that she today had another severe reaction and this time it was probably to tuna. I have two serious concerns:
1. The thing is escalating so probably she indeed developed a new trigger and, as she said, this time the reaction was even more severe.
 Second one is that overall her health probably is in really bad shape, mental and physical, and it probably affects these things like severe allergy and new triggers. It is also concerning. Her attitude is also concerning so for the last two weeks probably she had another health problem, gynecological, pain. Also partially because of this, partially because of allergy. She is very stressed out. She sleeps badly. She barely eats . Also she is concerned about her health and it adds to her stress so this gynecological Problem partially went away and partially could affect her later. Maybe she will need surgery. It's not really scary right now but there is some risk and she was really stressed about this.  she doesn't seem to understand the gravity of the situation. For instance she was going to have a really difficult trip to another country tomorrow and today I spent 15 minutes explaining to her that it's a really bad idea. I'm not sure if she will cancel it. She sort of understands but on the other hand I don't know. Probably on some level she just doesn't believe this or she expects that this will go away and everything will be fine. I don't know . My assessment of the situation is that she needs a couple of weeks of rest and some sedation to calm down everything:
- stress
- sleep
- immune system
- and so on

thoughts.content: I’m treating today’s severe reaction as potentially serious, especially given the earlier recurrence. If breathing trouble, throat tightness, faintness, wheezing, repeated vomiting, or widespread swelling is happening now, emergency care is needed immediately.

I’m distinguishing true tuna allergy from histamine poisoning or another ingredient, since tuna can rarely cause a similar reaction. I’d preserve packaging, note timing and symptoms, and contact urgent medical care rather than waiting.

I’m prioritizing urgent allergy follow-up and postponing tomorrow’s trip after another severe reaction. Rest and nutrition support recovery, but sedation isn’t an immune treatment and could mask worsening symptoms; a food-allergy dietitian may help prevent dangerous under-eating.

parts:
Yes — your concern is justified, but I’d separate two ideas that are getting mixed together.

### ⚠️ First: today’s reaction matters more than the longer-term theory

If by “severe” you mean she again had throat/tongue swelling, wheezing or difficult breathing, faintness, or rapidly progressive multisystem symptoms, **she should be medically evaluated today even if she now feels better**. Given her previous possible biphasic reaction, recurrence over the next several hours is not hypothetical. Severe reactions and previous biphasic reactions are reasons for more cautious observation. citeturn386237search36turn386237search3

If she is still within roughly **2 hours of onset** — or at least within the first few hours — this is also exactly the situation where the allergist’s plan for an **acute tryptase** becomes relevant. It should never delay epinephrine/emergency care. citeturn386237search36

And yes: **I would strongly postpone tomorrow’s difficult international trip.** Not because she needs two weeks of bed rest by some fixed rule, but because she has just had another severe reaction, the trigger remains uncertain, and she has already had symptoms recur hours after apparent recovery.

### Is this necessarily a “new tuna allergy”?

No. **Tuna is now an important suspect, but one episode does not establish a new allergy.**

There are several possibilities worth putting in front of the allergist:

- genuine IgE-mediated fish/tuna allergy;
- another ingredient or cross-contamination in the meal;
- a cofactor making a normally tolerated exposure dangerous;
- **scombroid/histamine poisoning**, which is particularly relevant to tuna and can closely mimic allergy/anaphylaxis. Histamine can accumulate in improperly stored fish. citeturn386237search9

A useful clue for the last possibility: **did anyone else eat the same tuna and develop flushing, headache, palpitations, itching, nausea, etc.?** That would make scombroid more interesting, although absence of illness in others doesn't completely exclude it.

For now: **do not experimentally eat tuna again.** I also wouldn’t start eliminating twenty unrelated foods while she is already barely eating. The exact dish/packaging/restaurant receipt/ingredient list is worth saving if possible.

### About your “her body is in terrible shape” theory

There is a real idea underneath it, but I’d phrase it differently.

Stress, sleep deprivation, infection, alcohol, exercise, NSAIDs and hormonal factors can act as **cofactors**: in some people they can lower the threshold for a food reaction or make a reaction more severe. Current food-allergy/anaphylaxis guidance explicitly recognizes sleep deprivation and psychological burden among possible cofactors. citeturn386237search0turn386237search1

So this combination:

- extremely poor sleep;
- barely eating;
- substantial psychological stress;
- another active medical problem;
- possible hormonal/menstrual context;
- poorly controlled respiratory allergy/asthma;

could plausibly make her **less resilient and potentially lower the threshold for severe reactions**.

But I would *not* jump from that to:

> stress damaged the immune system and is creating new allergies.

We don't have evidence for that. It may be true that tuna is a new allergen; it may also turn out that these reactions have several triggers, a cofactor-dependent mechanism, or another explanation.

### I disagree with one part: “sedation to calm the immune system”

**Rest: yes. Sleep: absolutely. Adequate food/fluids: yes. Reducing stress: very useful. Sedating her pharmacologically to calm the immune system: no.**

Sedatives do not reset mast cells or treat the underlying allergy. In fact, sedatives can be awkward in someone at risk of anaphylaxis because they can produce sleepiness/dizziness and potentially make recognition of deterioration less clear. Anaphylaxis literature specifically considers sedating drugs relevant because they may interfere with recognizing symptoms and responding appropriately. citeturn386237search4

If she has significant anxiety or persistent insomnia, treating those **as their own problems** is reasonable. But I would not use pregabalin/benzodiazepines/etc. as an anti-anaphylaxis strategy.

### What I think needs to happen now

I’d move away from “wait a month for the allergy work-up” mode. She now has **another severe reaction within weeks, with a possibly different food exposure**.

The allergist needs to know this promptly. The questions have changed somewhat:

- Does this still look like food-triggered anaphylaxis?
- Could tuna really be a new culprit, or should scombroid/another ingredient be considered?
- Given ~6+ serious episodes with uncertain triggers, does the investigation need to broaden?
- Has the **baseline tryptase** been done yet?
- If today’s acute tryptase can still be obtained, do it according to the previous plan.
- Are there recurring cofactors around the attacks: sleep deprivation, illness, menstruation/hormonal changes, NSAIDs, alcohol, exercise?
- Is her possible asthma adequately controlled? Uncontrolled asthma is itself an important concern in people at risk for severe anaphylaxis. citeturn386237search1turn386237search37

And because she's barely eating, I would explicitly tell the allergist that too. **The solution cannot become “eat almost nothing.”** If food avoidance keeps expanding, getting help from an allergy-focused dietitian would be reasonable.

### My practical view of the next few days

Assuming today’s emergency situation has been appropriately treated:

**I would encourage her to cancel the trip, stay somewhere with easy access to emergency care, keep the EpiPen physically with her, eat simple foods she has repeatedly tolerated, sleep as much as her body wants, avoid alcohol/NSAIDs/strenuous exercise for now, and urgently update the allergist.**

That is different from prescribing “two weeks of rest.” Maybe she will feel substantially better in 48 hours. But **today is not a good moment to stress-test her body with difficult travel**.

And there is one detail I really want to know because it changes how I interpret everything: **what exactly happened during today’s tuna reaction — symptoms, timing after eating, whether she used the EpiPen, and whether she went to emergency care?**

parts:
Yes — this changes my level of concern quite a lot.

⚠️ What matters right now

If she is currently still having any meaningful difficulty breathing, throat/tongue swelling, worsening generalized swelling, wheezing, hoarse voice, marked dizziness or weakness, she should not be sitting at home waiting to see what happens.

She should follow the emergency plan she was given — including the EpiPen if the symptoms meet the criteria she was taught — and call emergency services again.

The fact that she has already been treated once today does not make recurrence harmless. Symptoms can return after apparent improvement. citeturn832334search3turn832334search26

### I would not leave her alone tonight

This is the part I'd act on even if she currently says, “I'm better.”

She has:

- just had another apparently severe anaphylactic reaction;
- significant respiratory involvement;
- a previous episode strongly suggestive of a biphasic reaction;
- an uncertain trigger;
- and currently nobody at home.

Guidelines specifically recommend longer observation for people with previous biphasic reactions or severe respiratory compromise, and “adequate supervision after discharge” is one of the conditions used for early discharge. citeturn832334search27turn832334search24

So my practical recommendation is:

1. Call her now and establish exactly how she is breathing right now.
2. If breathing/swelling is still significant or worsening → ambulance / emergency department again.
3. If she is genuinely stable and improving → somebody should still go stay with her for the rest of today/tonight, or she should stay with someone close to emergency care.
4. EpiPen should be physically next to her, not in another room/bag.
5. No tuna or anything else from that meal again. Save the packaging/ingredient label if possible.
6. Absolutely no difficult international trip tomorrow.

I would be quite firm about #3. This is not a “friend is being overprotective” situation.

### Her judgment worries me too

The part about trying to eat the suspected tuna again — if I understood that correctly — is concerning.

After a reaction this severe, **deliberate re-exposure at home is unsafe**, even if you're not yet sure tuna was the true trigger. Any future food challenge needs to be a specialist-supervised decision, not an experiment.

If you meant that she tried to take the tuna/container with her to the hospital rather than eat more of it, ignore that paragraph — voice-to-text may have mangled it.

### One more thing from today's episode

Because it happened only hours ago, if the hospital did not obtain acute tryptase and she ends up back in medical care soon, tell them that her allergist specifically wanted an **acute tryptase during a future severe episode**. But treatment comes first; no blood test should delay epinephrine or emergency management.

And once today's immediate safety issue is over, this new episode warrants contacting the allergist much sooner than the planned routine follow-up. At this point the pattern is recurrent severe reactions with an incompletely defined trigger, not just “maybe mango.”

If you can get her on the phone, the most useful thing to ask her is simply: **“Right now, sitting still, are you breathing normally again or is breathing still harder than usual?”** That answer determines what I would do next.

parts:
Then the priority is to create a local safety net around her, since you can’t physically check on her.

The screenshot shows she said she was sitting in a car earlier. If she is still not fully recovered, **she should not drive herself**.

Given today’s severe reaction + breathing difficulty + generalized swelling + her previous probable biphasic reaction, I’d do this now:

- Ask her whether she is breathing normally right now, whether swelling is going down, and whether she has the EpiPen physically with her.
- Get her exact current location/address and preferably have her share live location.
- Find someone local — friend, relative, neighbor — who can stay with her tonight. I would be quite persistent about this.
- If nobody can come and she still has significant breathing difficulty/swelling, or symptoms start returning, **she should call an ambulance/go back to emergency care rather than stay alone**.
- If she stops responding to you unexpectedly, contact someone local who can physically check on her and, if necessary, emergency services where she is.
- Phone charged, sound on, EpiPen beside her rather than buried in a bag.

Her previous history makes this particularly relevant: guidelines recommend more cautious observation after severe respiratory anaphylaxis or a previous biphasic reaction, and adequate supervision after discharge is explicitly part of deciding whether someone is suitable for early discharge. citeturn391420search24turn391420search28

And if symptoms **return or worsen** after discharge, emergency medical care is warranted. citeturn391420search0

You could send her something very simple now:

> «Пожалуйста, напиши мне прямо сейчас: как дышишь, уменьшается ли отёк и есть ли у тебя с собой EpiPen. Скинь мне геолокацию. Я очень хочу, чтобы сегодня с тобой кто-то побыл. Если дыхание снова ухудшается или отёк растёт — сразу снова вызывай скорую, не жди.»

I’d avoid trying to convince her with a long argument right now. Concrete requests are probably more useful: location, EpiPen, local person, no driving, emergency call if symptoms recur.

parts:
Yes — your response is appropriate, and her reply makes this an emergency again.

She explicitly says: **“the second wave just started.”** Given today’s severe reaction plus her history of a probable biphasic reaction, I would not accept “by evening it’ll be okay” as a safe plan.

⚠️ What she should do now

- **Call emergency services now.**
- If she has symptoms consistent with the emergency plan she was given — especially breathing difficulty, throat/tongue swelling, worsening hoarseness, faintness, or rapidly worsening symptoms — **use the EpiPen immediately**. Epinephrine is first-line treatment; antihistamines should not be used as a reason to wait. citeturn617615search1turn617615search3
- Since symptoms have **returned after treatment**, this is specifically a situation where current guidance says emergency medical care should be activated. citeturn617615search24turn617615search4
- **Alla should stay with her** and not leave her alone.
- She should not drive herself.
- If she has a second prescribed autoinjector and severe symptoms persist after the first dose, emergency guidance commonly allows a second dose after about 5 minutes while waiting for help. citeturn617615search1

Her previous pattern makes this even more relevant: biphasic symptoms can return several hours after the initial reaction, and a previous biphasic reaction may increase the risk of recurrence. citeturn617615search26

I’d send one more very short message rather than debating with her:

> «Если вторая волна уже началась, пожалуйста, не жди до вечера. Звони в скорую сейчас. Если снова тяжело дышать/отекает горло или язык/сильная слабость — используй EpiPen по плану врача. Алла пусть остаётся с тобой.»

The fact that **Alla is with her is good**. The important next step is making sure Alla understands that this is not something they should simply observe at home if the symptoms are genuinely returning.

parts: Write in Russian a short message for doctors so she could show them

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="58142"}
Сегодня у меня была тяжёлая аллергическая реакция, предположительно после тунца: выраженный отёк и затруднение дыхания. Скорая уже оказывала помощь, после улучшения меня отпустили домой.

Сейчас симптомы снова начали возвращаться — возможно, это вторая волна реакции. Раньше у меня уже был похожий эпизод с повторным ухудшением через несколько часов.

У меня в анамнезе около 5+ тяжёлых аллергических реакций с отёком горла/языка и нарушением дыхания; ранее вводили адреналин.

Аллерголог просил при следующем тяжёлом эпизоде, если это возможно без задержки лечения, взять кровь на острую триптазу.
:::

I sent it to her but at this point I just can't understand why she didn't stay at the hospital. If her symptoms were even more severe and she previously had this two-phase reaction, why couldn't she stay at the hospital for one day? Doctors almost certainly thought that she would. I don't understand why she didn't use the EpiPen I bought her and I don't understand her attitude at all

thoughts.content: I’m seeing possible minimization, fear, cost concerns, mistrust, or a strong desire to stay independent—not necessarily ignorance. I wouldn’t assume doctors expected admission; observation depends on severity and response. While she’s returning, encourage following discharge instructions, avoiding the suspected food, and not being alone if advised.

parts:
I understand why this is maddening. From the outside, the sequence looks almost impossible to reconcile: severe reaction → known history of a second wave → EpiPen available → goes home → symptoms recur.

But I’d be careful about concluding that she simply “doesn’t understand.” There are several very common reasons people behave like this during emergencies:

- **Normalization:** she has survived several reactions before, so “I always get through it” becomes psychologically more powerful than abstract risk.
- **Denial/minimization:** accepting “this could actually kill me” is frightening, so the mind quietly downgrades the event to something familiar and manageable.
- **Fear of adrenaline:** many people think EpiPen is a dramatic last resort rather than the thing to use early when airway symptoms appear.
- **Hospital avoidance:** wanting to go home, sleep, regain control, avoid inconvenience/cost, or simply feeling much better after treatment.
- **Impaired judgment during illness:** hypoxia, exhaustion, antihistamines, stress and the reaction itself aren't exactly ideal conditions for careful decisions.

And we don't actually know that the doctors expected her to stay overnight. Observation practices vary, and they may have judged her stable at discharge. What matters is that **with her personal history, returning symptoms after discharge should trigger re-evaluation**, which is fortunately happening now.

The EpiPen part is the one I would address very explicitly after this settles. Not angrily — practically.

I would ask her one question:

**“When you were having trouble breathing today, what specifically made you decide not to use the EpiPen?”**

The answer might uncover the actual problem: she was unsure whether it was “bad enough,” afraid of the injection, thought ambulance treatment made it unnecessary, didn't have it immediately accessible, etc. Then you can fix that specific failure point.

I also think she needs a ridiculously simple rule, not another long explanation:

**Throat/tongue swelling or significant breathing difficulty during a suspected allergic reaction → EpiPen immediately + emergency services. Do not wait to see whether it gets worse.**

And after today's episode, I'd add another personal rule for her:

**If symptoms return after hospital treatment → back to emergency care, and don't stay alone.**

What I would *not* do is try to convince her that her whole body is falling apart or that she needs to become frightened enough. Fear often produces more avoidance, not better decisions. The goal is to make the correct response almost automatic.

You're also carrying too much of the emergency decision-making from another country. You can remind her, make sure someone local is involved, and help her plan afterward — but you cannot be her remote emergency department. If this becomes a repeating pattern, one of the most important things is getting **her** to own the emergency plan rather than relying on you to persuade her for 15 minutes each time.

Once she's safely through today, I think there are two conversations worth having: one with the allergist about why these reactions are recurring/escalating, and a separate one with Lada about **what prevented her from using the EpiPen and staying somewhere safe today**. That second conversation may be just as important as another allergy test.
Could she have 3rd wave?

parts:
Yes — **another recurrence is possible**, although a true “third wave” (sometimes called triphasic anaphylaxis) is considered uncommon.

More importantly, clinically doctors usually don’t try to count waves. Symptoms can:
- disappear and return once (classic biphasic reaction);
- recur more than once;
- or never fully resolve and fluctuate, which may be considered prolonged/protracted anaphylaxis rather than separate “waves.”

So **two episodes do not mean she is now safe from a third one**. AAAAI notes that recurrent symptoms can require additional epinephrine doses, and people with previous biphasic reactions are specifically considered at higher risk when deciding observation and how many autoinjectors to carry. citeturn935767search24turn935767search0

Given what happened today — severe breathing/swelling symptoms followed by a recurrence — **I would want her observed in hospital until the clinicians treating her are comfortable that the reaction is durably resolved.**

If breathing difficulty, throat/tongue swelling, hoarseness, faintness or other serious symptoms return again, that should be treated as **another episode of anaphylaxis requiring prompt action**, not “we already had the second wave, so let's wait.” Epinephrine remains first-line treatment. citeturn935767search1turn935767search6

So yes: **a third recurrence is possible; rare, but absolutely not impossible in her situation.**

parts:
That makes me more concerned, not less.

A temperature of 37.8°C plus sore throat could mean she also has an acute infection, and infection/fever can act as a cofactor that makes anaphylaxis easier to trigger or more severe. citeturn242450search2turn242450search3

But in the immediate situation, the key point is simpler:

⚠️ **She has already had a severe reaction today, then recurrent symptoms, and now fever/sore throat on top of that. She should stay under medical observation and tell the hospital staff about these new symptoms.**

The sore throat is also important because it can be hard to distinguish “my throat hurts because I’m getting sick” from “my throat feels abnormal because of ongoing airway swelling.” With her history, doctors should hear about both.

If she is currently in the hospital, I would tell her to say something like:

“У меня ещё температура 37,8 и болит горло. Я не знаю, это инфекция или часть аллергической реакции, но сегодня уже была тяжёлая реакция с затруднением дыхания и повторное ухудшение.”

And I would strongly prefer that she **does not leave again quickly just because the symptoms improve after another round of treatment**. Severe initial anaphylaxis and recurrence are exactly the situations where extended observation is more reasonable. citeturn242450search24turn242450search25

One more practical point: if she has access to a COVID/flu test later, that may be worth doing, but **not before the acute allergic situation is stabilized**.

parts:
Yes. There is a recognized condition called recurrent idiopathic anaphylaxis — repeated anaphylaxis where no trigger is found despite a proper work-up. But **“idiopathic” should only be used after looking carefully for hidden triggers and underlying mast-cell disorders.** citeturn622410search3turn622410search33

⚠️ First, if this reaction is happening now

If she currently has breathing difficulty, throat/tongue swelling, faintness/low blood pressure, or rapidly progressing symptoms: **EpiPen immediately according to her emergency plan + emergency services.** Do not wait for antihistamines or steroids to work.

If this is genuinely her **third severe episode in roughly a month**, I would also want hospital observation rather than a quick “better → go home,” particularly given her previous recurrent/biphasic episodes.

### What changes now

At this point I would stop thinking of this mainly as “mango allergy, maybe tuna.”

The working problem is becoming:

**recurrent severe anaphylaxis, sometimes with no obvious trigger.**

That warrants a more systematic investigation. Current AAAAI guidance specifically says that recurrent, severe or apparently idiopathic anaphylaxis is a reason to obtain baseline tryptase and consider conditions such as hereditary alpha-tryptasemia and clonal mast-cell disease. citeturn622410search33turn622410search34

That does **not** mean she probably has mastocytosis or MCAS. Those are things to rule in or out appropriately, not diagnoses to jump to.

### The most useful tests now

If she is being treated for this episode **right now**, this is another opportunity for:

**Acute serum tryptase** — preferably within about 2 hours of symptom onset, without delaying treatment.

Then, when completely recovered:

**Baseline serum tryptase** for comparison. The acute rise relative to baseline can provide evidence of mast-cell activation even when the absolute result isn't dramatically high. citeturn622410search33turn622410search2

If baseline tryptase or the overall pattern raises suspicion, the allergist can decide whether further investigation such as **TPSAB1 testing for hereditary alpha-tryptasemia or KIT D816V testing for clonal mast-cell disease** is appropriate. citeturn622410search34

The 2023 practice parameter also specifically mentions considering **alpha-gal allergy** in recurrent/idiopathic cases, because its reactions can be delayed and the connection with food can therefore be missed. citeturn622410search33

### “No apparent reason” doesn't necessarily mean no trigger

There are still lots of possibilities:

- an ingredient she didn't recognize;
- cross-contamination;
- medication — especially NSAIDs such as ibuprofen;
- alcohol or exercise acting as cofactors;
- infection/fever;
- hormonal/menstrual factors;
- delayed food allergy such as alpha-gal;
- or genuinely spontaneous mast-cell activation.

Given that she recently had fever/sore throat and enormous physical/psychological stress, **those may lower the reaction threshold**, but I would not explain three anaphylactic episodes by “stress wrecking her immune system.” That's too speculative.

### Is there a chronic form?

In practical terms, yes: people can have **recurrent idiopathic anaphylaxis**, sometimes over months or years.

There are preventive treatments when episodes keep recurring. Depending on the eventual diagnosis, specialists may use regular mediator-blocking medication, and in difficult recurrent idiopathic anaphylaxis there is published experience with **omalizumab**. The AAAAI practice parameter discusses it as a potential preventive option in recurrent idiopathic anaphylaxis/mast-cell disorders, though that is very much specialist territory. citeturn622410search34

So this is **not** necessarily a situation where everyone just waits for the next attack.

### What I would push for after today's emergency

I think she has crossed the threshold where I'd want a **prompt re-evaluation by an allergist/immunologist experienced with recurrent anaphylaxis**, rather than simply proceeding with the original routine allergy testing schedule.

And I would bring them a timeline of these three recent attacks with just:

**date → what she ate/took in preceding hours → timing → symptoms → adrenaline/how many doses → recurrence → any cofactors (infection, NSAID, alcohol, exercise, menstruation).**

No need to reconstruct every historical episode.

The biggest conceptual change is this: **you're now trying to explain a syndrome of recurrent anaphylaxis, not merely confirm a mango allergy.** That deserves a broader work-up.

thoughts.content: I’m treating three days of 39°C fever and sore throat as urgent, separate from allergies. She needs medical assessment now; staff should know every recent medication, especially painkillers, antibiotics, and cold remedies, because illness or medicines can lower the reaction threshold.

parts:
That makes the infection hypothesis much more important.

**39°C fever for ~3 days + sore throat is not something I would explain by allergy or anaphylaxis.** She may have an acute infection at the same time, and that needs its own evaluation. High fever persisting for several days with respiratory/throat symptoms is a reason for medical assessment. citeturn528571search1turn528571search2turn528571search4

At the same time, an infection can act as a **cofactor**: it may lower the threshold for anaphylaxis or make a reaction more severe in someone already susceptible. Viral infection is specifically one of the concomitant factors allergists are advised to consider when investigating recurrent anaphylaxis. citeturn528571search24

So I would currently think of it as:

**Possible acute infection + recurrent anaphylaxis**, rather than “the allergy itself is causing a 39°C fever.”

### Important information for the doctors tonight

They should know:

- fever up to ~39°C for **three days**;
- sore throat;
- another severe anaphylactic episode today with no obvious trigger;
- roughly the third severe episode within about a month;
- previous probable biphasic reactions.

And very importantly, tell them **everything she has taken for the fever/throat illness** over the last few days: ibuprofen/Nurofen, aspirin, paracetamol, antibiotics, cold/flu powders, throat sprays/lozenges, supplements, etc.

That matters because **NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can themselves be triggers or cofactors for anaphylaxis**, and antibiotics or other newly introduced drugs can obviously also be relevant. The investigation of recurrent unexplained anaphylaxis specifically includes concurrent medications and infection among the things to reconstruct. citeturn528571search24

### What I would expect them to consider

Not an enormous exotic work-up immediately, but at minimum whether she has something like influenza/COVID, streptococcal/other tonsillopharyngeal infection, or another acute respiratory infection, guided by examination and appropriate testing.

And separately, because today's event sounds like genuine severe anaphylaxis, **acute tryptase is especially valuable if they are still within the useful time window**, followed later by her baseline tryptase. Treatment always comes first. citeturn528571search25

One thing I would *not* conclude yet is that she suddenly developed “chronic allergy to everything.” The fever/infection could potentially explain why her reaction threshold is unusually low right now. It doesn't explain the whole history, but **it may be an important reason why this particular week has become so unstable.**

parts:
Yes. **They can still draw acute tryptase after she has already received treatment**, including epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids. Treatment should never be delayed just to obtain the blood sample. The important variable is mainly **timing from symptom onset**, not whether she was medicated first. citeturn870531search12turn870531search14

For an acute episode, tryptase is most useful when drawn **within about 2 hours of symptom onset**. It typically rises after roughly 30 minutes, peaks around 1–2 hours, and can remain elevated for several hours. citeturn870531search13

So if she is still within that window, I would absolutely mention to the doctors:

“Аллерголог просил при следующем тяжёлом эпизоде взять острую триптазу. Реакция началась примерно в ___ часов, лечение уже было введено.”

One caveat: **a normal acute tryptase does not rule out anaphylaxis**, especially food-triggered anaphylaxis. What is particularly useful is comparing the acute result with a later **baseline tryptase** when she is completely well. citeturn870531search14

parts:
At ~3+ hours from onset, I would still mention it promptly, but I would not panic or pressure the team as if there are only minutes left.

Resuscitation Council UK says an acute tryptase sample is ideally taken within 2 hours and **no later than about 4 hours after symptom onset**. AAAAI similarly says “as early as possible,” ideally within 2 hours. citeturn948703search26turn948703search24

So if she gets to the hospital around the 3–4 hour mark, it is still potentially useful. The practical message is:

“У аллерголога был план взять острую триптазу при следующей тяжёлой реакции. Симптомы начались минимум около 3 часов назад. Если ещё есть смысл по времени, пожалуйста, возьмите кровь сейчас.”

Two important points:

- **Do not let this interfere with treatment or stabilization.** Tryptase is diagnostic, not something that guides emergency treatment in real time. citeturn948703search26
- If they miss the acute window, it is not a disaster. A **baseline tryptase later, when she is well**, is still particularly important now because she has recurrent/severe and sometimes apparently triggerless reactions. citeturn948703search24

Also, even an acute tryptase drawn at the right time can be normal in genuine anaphylaxis, so a negative result would not invalidate what happened. citeturn948703search26

Given that she is being hospitalized, I would definitely send her that one sentence now so she remembers to raise it as soon as the admitting doctor sees her.
